newsitem.title: USA: NYC one-shots to hit $1.6 bln in FY 1998--watchdog.
newsitem.headline: NYC one-shots to hit $1.6 bln in FY 1998--watchdog.

text.p: The New York State Financial Control Board, created in the mid-1970s to help New York City out of a fiscal crisis, on Tuesday said that the city was relying on nearly $1.6 billion of one-shots in fiscal 1998.

The monitor, which faulted the city for huge, looming budget gaps, which will exceed $3 billion in fiscal 2000, said relying on one-shots impeded efforts to close such gaps. "The ongoing use of this level of non-recurring resources to balance the city budget undermines progress towards structural balance," said the Financial Control Board.

The monitor estimated that debt service, when measured as a percentage of tax revenues, will slip to just over 14 percent in fiscal 1998, down from about 18 percent in the previous period, in part because the Giuliani Administration plans to use a $391 million surplus to prepay debt.
However, this gauge climbs to about 18.8 percent in fiscal 1999 to 2001, the control board said in its latest report.
Alan Hevesi, the city comptroller, has said that while 15 percent is a typical yardstick used to measure how much debt a locality can afford, New York City can tolerate about 18 percent.

The board recommended that the city adopt a written policy for debt, which spells out upper limits for debt and debt service, requires pay-as-you-go financing for part of the capital plan, and sets "crucial priorities" for capital and budget programs.
